Take-home Exercise 2

Jeounghyun Kim

Published

March 2, 2025

Singapore’s International Trade Analysis

1. Overview

1.1 Introduction

Merchandise trade is one of the commonly used indicators of economic performance, for Singapore, international trade is crucial to its economy. In the context of shifting global dynamics of trade due to geopolitical events and economic policies, it becomes imperative to analyse and visualise trade trends in a meaningful manner.

In this take-home piece, we aim to improve the understanding of Singapore’s merchandise trade data through the use of data graphics by checking three existing visualizations, and thereafter, proposing better ones utilizing ggplot2 and other R packages. By identifying the strengths and limitations of the original charts, we will apply appropriate visualization techniques to improve clarity, comparability, and insight generation.

Additionally, we will conduct a time-series analysis or forecasting to uncover trade patterns over the years, offering a deeper understanding of Singapore’s trade performance. This exercise will not only refine data visualization skills but also provide valuable insights into Singapore’s trade landscape.

1.2 The Data

The data for this analysis is sourced from Singapore’s Merchandise Trade by Region/Market, retrieved from the Department of Statistics Singapore (DOS) via the SingStat website. This dataset captures Singapore’s trade activities across various sectors and time periods.

In this study, we examine three major datasets:

  • Total Merchandise Trade (2020-2024): Value of all imports and exports of goods at current prices, the monthly series measures long term trends in trade.

  • Non-Oil Domestic Exports (2024): DATA Export data by major commodity sections excluding oil-related trade; Used to Study the Composition of Singapore’s Exports

  • Overall Exports and Imports of Services (2020-2024): Tracks the total value of traded services, offering insights into Singapore’s trade performance over the past five years.

To ensure data clarity and accuracy, additional computed columns and non-relevant metadata were removed during preprocessing.

2. Getting started

2.1 Load Packages

Load the following R packages using the pacman::p_load() function to streamline the workflow:

  • readxl: Enables reading Excel files into R for data analysis.

  • tidyverse: A core collection of R packages for data science, including:

    • dplyr (data manipulation)

    • ggplot2 (data visualization)

    • tidyr (data tidying)

  • tsibble: Provides tools for handling and analyzing time-series data.

  • feasts: A package for time series visualization and feature extraction.

  • fable: Used for forecasting time-series data using statistical models.

  • seasonal: Facilitates seasonal adjustment of time series data.

  • treemap: Creates treemap visualizations for hierarchical data.

  • plotly: Enables interactive visualizations for data exploration.

  • scales: Enhances ggplot2 with functions for formatting axes, labels, and colors.

  • RColorBrewer: Provides color palettes for visually appealing data visualizations.

By leveraging these packages, we ensure efficient data handling, visualization, and analysis throughout this study.

pacman::p_load(readxl, tidyverse, tsibble, feasts, fable, seasonal, treemap, plotly, scales, RColorBrewer)

3. Data Visualization

3.1 Total Merchandise Trade at Current Prices, 2020 - 2024

Current Chart Analysis Pros and Cons

The original visualization used a horizontal bar chart to display annual trade values, making year-to-year comparisons clear. However, it lacked a clear representation of trade trends and balance over time.

Proposed Improvements

The revised chart combines a stacked bar chart with trend lines to provide a clearer overview of trade patterns. The stacked bars maintain the distinction between exports and imports, while the trend lines enhance visibility of trade fluctuations. This approach improves interpretability and makes it easier to identify trade growth and balance.

Implementation

The new visualization was created using ggplot2 in R. geom_bar() was used for the stacked bars, while geom_line() and geom_point() were added to highlight trade trends.

3.1.2 Visualisation

df_long <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -Category, names_to = "Month", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(substr(Month, 1, 4))) %>%  
  group_by(Year, Category) %>%
  summarise(Total_Trade = sum(Value), .groups = "drop")

p <- ggplot(df_long, aes(x = Year, y = Total_Trade, fill = Category)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +  
  geom_line(aes(group = 1, color = "Total Trade"), size = 1.2) + # Total Trade Line
  geom_point(aes(color = "Total Trade"), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "tomato"), 
                    labels = c("Exports", "Imports")) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black"), 
                     labels = c("Exports Trend", "Imports Trend")) +  
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(scale = 1e-6)) +  
  labs(title = "Total Merchandise Trade (2020 - 2024)",
       x = "Year", y = "Trade Value (Million SGD)", 
       fill = "Trade Type", color = "Trend Line") +  
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        text = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 12),  
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10))  

p_interactive <- ggplotly(p)
p_interactive

3.2. Non-Oil domestic Exports by Major Commodity Sections, 2024

Current Chart Analysis Pros and Cons

The original chart is ship-based infographic, so the idea of an export is visually intuitive. Different commodity categories are distinguished by unique icons and color-coded sections. However, the ratios of export values are not represented accurately and hence it is difficult to make comparisons. Label placement is also cluttered, making it non-readable.

Proposed Improvements

As such, a treemap guarantees that each category is simultaneously represented in proportion to the area it occupies, enabling greater accuracy in comparison. This also decreases visual clutter and still keeps a structured layout.

Implementation

The revised chart was created using ggplot2 and treemapify in R. Each category is represented proportionally, with labels placed inside for clarity. A color gradient enhances readability, making larger export categories stand out.

3.2.1 Import data & Data Preprocessing

file_path <- "non_oil_domestic_exports_2024.xlsx"
data <- read_excel(file_path)

data$Value <- data$`2024 Total` / 1e6  

summary(data$Value)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.1749  2.6732 10.5734 19.2890 28.6450 70.3791 
data$Percentage <- round((data$Value / sum(data$Value)) * 100, 1)

data$Label <- paste0(data$Category, "\n", round(data$Value, 1), "B S$ (", round(data$Percentage, 1), "%)")

3.2.2 Visualisation

treemap(data,
        index = "Label",          
        vSize = "Value",          
        vColor = "Value",         
        type = "manual",          
        palette = brewer.pal(9, "Blues"),  
        algorithm = "pivotSize",  
        sortID = "Value",         
        title = "Singapore Non-Oil Domestic Exports (2024)",  
        title.legend = "Export Value (B S$)",  
        fontsize.labels = 12,     
        fontcolor.labels = "white", 
        align.labels = list(c("center", "center")))

3.3 Overall Exports and Imports of Services (2020-2024)

Current Chart Analysis

The original visualization uses horizontal bars with container-themed elements to represent exports and imports over time. Althought great looking, the design fails at communicating trends in trade. Having one bar for every year makes visibility of patterns over time difficult, and the decorative lines add nothing of value.

Proposed Improvements

Instead, a stacked bar chart with trend lines is a better option. This format allows for both explicit year-on-year comparisons and emphasizes the international relationship of exports to imports. Interpretability is further improved by trend lines that show global growth tendencies.

Implementation

The revised chart was created using ggplot2 in R. geom_bar() was used for stacked bars, with geom_line() and geom_point() overlaying trade trends. Custom colors and labels improve readability while maintaining a clean, data-focused design.

ggplot() +
  geom_bar(data = data_long, aes(x = factor(Years), y = Value, fill = Category), stat = "identity") +
  
  geom_text(data = data_long, aes(x = factor(Years), y = Value, label = Value), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 4, color = "white", fontface = "bold") +

  
  geom_line(data = data, aes(x = factor(Years), y = `Exports (S$ Bil)`, group = 1, color = "Exports"), 
            size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  geom_point(data = data, aes(x = factor(Years), y = `Exports (S$ Bil)`, color = "Exports"), size = 3) +  

  #import trend line
  geom_line(data = data, aes(x = factor(Years), y = `Imports (S$ Bil)`, group = 1, color = "Imports"), 
            size = 1.5, linetype = "solid") +
  geom_point(data = data, aes(x = factor(Years), y = `Imports (S$ Bil)`, color = "Imports"), size = 3) +  

  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Exports (S$ Bil)" = export_bar_color, 
                               "Imports (S$ Bil)" = import_bar_color)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Exports" = export_trend_color, 
                                "Imports" = import_trend_color)) +

  labs(title = "Overall Exports and Imports of Services (2020-2024)",
       x = "Year", y = "S$ Billion",
       fill = "Category", color = "Trend") +
  theme_minimal()

4. Time-series analysis

4.1 Getting Started

pacman::p_load(readr,tidyverse, tsibble, feasts, fable, seasonal)

4.2 Importing the data

First, read_csv() of readr package is used to import Import_Export.csv file into R environment.
The imported file is saved as a tibble object called ts_data.

ts_data <- read_csv(
  "Import_Export.csv")

In the code chunk below, parse_date_time() of lubridate package is used to convert the data type of “Data Series”field from Character to Date.

library(lubridate)

ts_data$`Data Series` <- parse_date_time(ts_data$`Data Series`, orders = "Y b")

4.2.3 Converting tibble object to tsibbleobject

The code chunk below converting ts_data from tibble object into tsibble object by using as_tsibble() of tsibble R package.

ts_tsibble <- ts_data %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(`Data Series`)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)

What can we learn from the code chunk above? + mutate() of dplyrpackage is used to derive a new field by transforming the data values in Month-Year field into month-year format. The transformation is performed by using yearmonth() of tsibble package. + as_tsibble() is used to convert the tibble data frame into tsibble data frame.

4.3 Visualising Time-series Data

In order to visualise the time-series data effectively, we need to organise the data frame from wide to long format by using pivot_longer() of tidyr package as shown below.

ts_longer <- ts_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(2:34),
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade")

4.3.1 Visualising single time-series: ggplot2 methods

The code chunk below demonstrates how to visualize the trade trend of the United States over time using ggplot2.

ts_longer %>%
  filter(Country == "United States") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Data Series`, 
             y = Trade))+
  geom_line(size = 0.5)

This visualization provides insights into the trade volume fluctuations of the United States, helping to identify trends, seasonality, and any significant changes over time.

Interpretation: We observe an upward trend in import trade volume over time, although with considerable year-to-year volatility. The abrupt jumps and seasonal patterns indicate the influences of dynamics external to trade itself, such as global economic conditions, trade policies, and economic crises (e.g. COVID-19 influences on trade).

More developed analysis to seasonal decomposition or time-series forecasting (ARIMA models) can be done for predicting the future trading and drivers causing such price variations.

4.3.2 Plotting multiple time-series data with ggplot2 methods

ggplot(data = ts_longer, 
       aes(x = `Data Series`, 
           y = Trade,
           color = Country)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", 
        legend.box.spacing = unit(0.5, "cm"))

In order to provide effective comparison, facet_wrap() of ggplot2package is used to create small multiple line graph also known as trellis plot.

ggplot(data = ts_longer, 
       aes(x = `Data Series`, 
           y = Trade)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ Country,  
             ncol = 3,   
             scales = "free_y") +  
  theme_bw()

Interpretation: The United States trade volume shows a steady upward trend with fluctuations, indicating seasonal patterns and external economic influences. Compared to Total All Markets, U.S. trade remains significant but follows global trade trends. Further analysis could explore seasonal impacts and future forecasts.

4.4 Visual Analysis of Time-series Data

Time-series datasets often exhibit seasonal components, where patterns repeat periodically (e.g., monthly or yearly cycles). These cycles can sometimes obscure the underlying trend when forecasting but can also serve as a strong signal for predictive models.

tsibble_longer <- ts_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(2:34),
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade")

19.4.1 Visual Analysis of Seasonality with Seasonal Plot

A seasonal plot is similar to a time plot except that the data are plotted against the individual seasons in which the data were observed.

tsibble_longer %>%
  filter(Country == "United States" |
         Country == "Total All Markets") %>% 
  gg_season(Trade)

Interpretation: The United States trade volume shows seasonal patterns, with peaks around mid-year and declines at year-end. Trade has grown over time, with recent years showing higher volumes than earlier periods.

tsibble_longer %>%
  filter(Country %in% c("Total All Markets", "United States")) %>% 
  gg_subseries(Trade)

Interpretation: The subseries plot confirms monthly variations, where mid-year months tend to have higher trade levels. The overall upward trend indicates consistent trade growth over time.

4.5 Time series decomposition

4.5.1 Single time series decomposition

tsibble_longer %>%
  filter(`Country` == "United States") %>%
  PACF(Trade) %>% 
  autoplot()

Interpretation:

  • The PACF plot shows significant spikes at lag 1 and lag 2, indicating that the previous month’s trade values strongly influence the current month’s trade volume.

  • A gradual decline in PACF suggests the potential need for an AR(1) or AR(2) component in an ARIMA model.

  • The presence of seasonal lags (e.g., around lag 12) suggests a possible yearly seasonality effect in trade data.

4.6 Visual STL Diagnostics

tsibble_longer %>%
  filter(`Country` == "United States") %>%
  model(stl = STL(Trade)) %>%
  components() %>%
  autoplot()

Interpretation:

  • The trend component shows a long-term increasing trend, with notable fluctuations over the years.

  • The seasonal component reveals a consistent repeating pattern, indicating that trade volume follows a predictable seasonal cycle each year.

  • The remainder component represents unexplained variations (residuals), with some spikes likely due to external economic events or policy changes affecting trade.

5. Conclusion

The trade restructuring cum globalisation, especially against the backdrop of the Trump administration, has huge impact on Singapore trade. Protectionist measures including increased tariffs and reconfiguration of supply chains are making trade flows more volatile, which has been exacerbated by external shocks like COVID-19.

While a time-series analysis shows a general upward trend in Singapore’s trade with the U.S. over the long term, there are also clear seasonal patterns and short-term fluctuations. STL decomposition highlights a recurrent seasonal cycle, indicating that trade volumes follow a predictable annual pattern. The PACF analysis shows strong correlations at shorter lags, reinforcing the idea that prior trade volumes significantly impact future trends. These findings suggest that Singapore’s trade performance remains highly sensitive to external economic conditions and policy changes.

To build economic resilience, Singapore must diversify its trade relationships beyond its major trading partners, notably the United States. By diversifying its portfolio to more emerging markets and investing in high-value sectors including digital trade and financial services, Singapore should be able to solidify its comparative advantage. The factors influencing trade have shifted dramatically over the last 15 years or so, due to rapid advances in technology and changing worker demographics.
